qs.q: A neonate presents with recurrent chest infections and choking on feeds, but initial routine nasogastric tube placement passed easily into the stomach without meeting resistance. Antenatal history revealed no polyhydramnios. What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Pure oesophageal atresia with a long gap
Oesophageal atresia with a distal fistula
Atresia with a proximal pouch fistula
H-type tracheo-oesophageal fistula
qs.e: An H-type fistula involves an isolated tracheo-oesophageal fistula without atresia, presenting later in life with recurrent respiratory symptoms rather than immediate neonatal drooling or a blocked tube. Atresia variants always prevent standard nasogastric tube passage.
qs.s: Oesophageal Atresia and Tracheo-oesophageal Fistula: MCQs

qs.q: A pregnant woman undergoes a routine second-trimester ultrasound which reveals polyhydramnios and an absent stomach bubble. Which congenital anomaly of the fetus is most strongly suggested by this sonographic finding?
o: Congenital duodenal atresia
Congenital oesophageal atresia
Congenital tracheomalacia
Congenital diaphragmatic hernia
qs.e: Inability of the fetus to swallow amniotic fluid due to oesophageal atresia leads to polyhydramnios and a small or absent stomach bubble. Duodenal atresia typically presents with a double bubble sign rather than a completely absent stomach bubble.
qs.s: Oesophageal Atresia and Tracheo-oesophageal Fistula: MCQs

qs.q: A 3-day-old term neonate presents with persistent bilious vomiting and a soft, flat abdomen since birth. The mother had polyhydramnios during pregnancy. A plain abdominal radiograph demonstrates a 'double bubble' sign with a complete absence of distal bowel gas. Which of the following is the most likely underlying mechanism?
o: An in utero mesenteric vascular accident causing ischaemic resorption
Abnormal rotation and fixation resulting in Ladd's bands obstruction
Failure of recanalisation of the solid cord of the embryonic duodenum
Midgut volvulus with vascular compromise around the superior mesenteric artery
qs.e: Duodenal atresia is caused by the failure of recanalisation of the solid cord of the duodenum during the 8th to 10th weeks of gestation. Jejunal and ileal atresias, by contrast, are typically caused by in utero mesenteric vascular accidents.
qs.s: Intestinal Malrotation and Intestinal Atresia in Children: MCQs

qs.q: A 1-day-old neonate presents with non-bilious vomiting shortly after feeding, along with a maternal history of polyhydramnios. Imaging reveals a double bubble sign. The level of the obstruction is most likely located at which anatomical site?
o: At the duodenojejunal flexure near the ligament of Treitz
Proximal to the ampulla of Vater in the duodenum
Within the proximal jejunum after the ligament of Treitz
Distal to the ampulla of Vater in the second part of the duodenum
qs.e: Duodenal obstruction proximal to the ampulla of Vater typically presents with non-bilious vomiting, whereas lesions distal to the ampulla present with bilious vomiting. Both can produce a double bubble radiographic sign.
qs.s: Intestinal Malrotation and Intestinal Atresia in Children: MCQs

qs.q: A newborn presents with severe watery diarrhea from day one of life, accompanied by polyhydramnios and metabolic acidosis. Laboratory tests show hyponatremia. The condition is linked to a mutation in the SPINT2 gene. What is the diagnosis?
o: Congenital Chloride Diarrhea
Monosaccharide Malabsorption
Congenital Sodium Diarrhea
Intestinal Epithelial Dysplasia
qs.e: Congenital sodium diarrhea is an autosomal recessive disease caused by a defect in jejunal sodium/proton exchange linked to the SPINT2 gene, featuring hyponatremia and metabolic acidosis. Chloride diarrhea presents with metabolic alkalosis and high fecal chloride.
qs.s: Approach to a child with diarrhea & constipation: MCQs
